case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that because parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody and management of their children, a preponderance standard in a permanent neglect proceeding violates due process and a State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky is the federal constitutional floor for every termination of parental rights in Missouri and the source of the clear, cogent and convincing standard in section 211.447.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding, and left the decision whether counsel is required to be made case by case by the trial court subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Lassiter is the federal baseline on counsel in termination cases, and it is the reason Missouri's statutory right under section 211.462.2 matters so much in practice.
key_cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of the mother's parental rights, holding that substantial evidence supported the statutory grounds under section 211.447.5(2) and (3), including that a parent's mental condition must be assessed by evidence of conduct at the time of the termination hearing and not merely when jurisdiction was taken.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Missouri Supreme Court's current statement of the evidentiary threshold for terminating parental rights and of the requirement that unfitness be measured at the time of the termination hearing.
key_cases.quote: To terminate parental rights, the trial court must find clear, cogent and convincing evidence of at least one of the grounds of termination outlined in section 211.447.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination and held that Missouri's two-tier scheme — clear, cogent and convincing evidence of a statutory ground, then a preponderance of the evidence on best interests — comports with due process under Santosky v. Kramer.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Missouri authority on which burden of proof applies to each half of a termination judgment and on why the lower best-interests standard survives constitutional challenge.
key_cases.quote: After a ground for termination has been shown, section 211.447 requires that termination be found in the child's best interest by a preponderance of the evidence standard of proof.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination, holding that proof of only one statutory ground by clear, cogent and convincing evidence sustains the judgment, that such findings are reviewed under Murphy v. Carron, and that best interests is proved by a preponderance at trial and reviewed for abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: P.L.O. is the leading Missouri statement of the standard of proof and standard of review that govern every contested termination and appeal from one.
key_cases.quote: On that question, the standard of proof at trial is a preponderance of the evidence, and the standard of review on appeal is abuse of discretion.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, rejecting a vagueness challenge to section 211.447.5(6)(a) because the statutory limitation that incarceration alone is not a ground applies only to the subsections it names and not to an unfitness finding under 211.447.5(6)(a).
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Missouri authority on how an incarcerated parent's conduct may support a finding of unfitness notwithstanding the statutory caution that incarceration alone is not a ground.
key_cases.quote: By the statute's plain terms, subdivision (6) of § 211.447.7 applies only to termination that is pursuant to certain subsections or subdivisions.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of the mother's parental rights and remanded, holding that past acts support termination only when convincingly linked to predicted future harm, that findings supporting the earlier assumption of jurisdiction must be updated to describe the parent's condition at the time of the termination hearing, and that the trial court's findings here were insufficient on every ground relied on.
key_cases.relevance: K.A.W. is the leading modern Missouri Supreme Court decision on what a termination judgment must actually find, and it is the parent-side counterweight to the affirmances that dominate this node.
key_cases.quote: To that end, a trial court cannot support a termination by merely incorporating earlier findings supporting its assumption of jurisdiction or some other earlier disposition.

key_cases.holding: The Court construed Rule 73.01 to mean that the judgment in a court-tried case will be sustained unless there is no substantial evidence to support it, it is against the weight of the evidence, it erroneously declares the law, or it erroneously applies the law, and directed that the labels 'de novo' and 'clearly erroneous' no longer be used.
key_cases.relevance: Every sufficiency challenge to a Missouri termination judgment is decided under this standard, which P.L.O. and T.W.C. in this brief invoke by name without citing it.
key_cases.quote: The use of the words de novo and clearly erroneous is no longer appropriate in appellate review of cases under Rule 73.01.
